standard.title: Continuities and Changes in an Asian Society Around 1900
standard.description: continuities and changes and their effects on the ways of life and living conditions, political and legal institutions, and cultural expression around the turn of the 20th century in an Asian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the features of the selected Asian society before European contact (K19), the causes and effects of that contact (K20), and key events and figures in the society's development (K21). This descriptor synthesises this knowledge into a continuity/change analysis of the society around 1900 — the period when imperial pressure was most intense.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine continuities and changes and their effects on ways of life, political institutions, and cultural expression in the selected Asian society around the turn of the 20th century.

nodes.label: The society's position and the challenge of foreign influence around 1900
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the position of the selected Asian society in relation to other nations around the turn of the 20th century, including how increasing foreign influence was challenging and changing the society.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how foreign influence was challenging or changing the selected Asian society around 1900.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the position of the selected Asian society in relation to other nations around 1900 including the influence of nationalist ideas; describe how increasing foreign influence and imperialism was challenging the society — for China, the development of steam-powered factories and military technology; for Japan, the accelerating Meiji modernisation and emergence as a regional power; for India, the maturation of the British Raj; for Indonesia, the Cultivation System and Ethical System under Dutch colonial administration.
wider: Compare how two different Asian societies responded to the pressure of Western imperialism around 1900 — one through deliberate modernisation on Western terms (Meiji Japan) and one through attempted resistance within traditional frameworks (Qing China) — assessing the different outcomes produced by different responses

Examine how the development of steam-powered military technology shifted the balance of power between Asian societies and European colonial powers — analysing why military modernisation became central to the question of sovereignty

response_modes.reason: Situating the selected society in relation to other nations — not just European powers but also other Asian societies — prevents a simple coloniser/colonised binary and shows how Asian societies were also in competition and comparison with each other.

success_criteria: Explains the position of the selected Asian society in the world around 1900, including the main external pressures it faced
Describes at least two ways foreign influence was challenging or changing the society at this time

nodes.label: What changed and what remained — using the continuity/change framework
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate what remained the same and what changed in the selected Asian society as a result of contact with European powers, applying the continuity/change framework across ways of life, political institutions, and cultural expression.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one significant continuity and one significant change in the selected Asian society around 1900, explaining why each occurred.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate what remained the same or changed during this period as a result of European contact — for India: the Raj and British influences on society (roads, railways, education, law) alongside the persistence of Indian cultural and religious life; for Japan: the Meiji modernisation — adopting Western military, legal, and industrial models — alongside deliberate preservation of Japanese cultural and national identity; for Indonesia: comparing the Cultivation System and Ethical System to examine how colonial policy changed over time while Dutch control continued.
wider: Examine the Meiji Restoration as a deliberate management of change and continuity — investigating what Japanese leaders chose to adopt from Western models and what they determined should be preserved as distinctively Japanese

Compare the Cultivation System and Ethical System in the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia) to examine how colonial policy could 'change' while the fundamental relationship of colonial exploitation remained continuous

Investigate how ordinary people in the selected Asian society experienced continuity and change differently from the political elite — examining whether changes in governance and economy affected daily cultural and social life at the village or community level

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the full knowledge of the selected Asian society — requiring students to synthesise understanding of features (K19), contact effects (K20), and key events (K21) into a structured continuity/change analysis.

success_criteria: Identifies and explains at least two continuities and two changes in the selected Asian society around 1900
Explains at least one change in terms of ways of life, political institutions, or cultural expression
